conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you so much for making time for this today. My name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in postpartum mental health. I’m here to help you settle into new motherhood by checking in on how things have felt for you lately.

We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) to screen for any symptoms of depression or anxiety that can pop up after a baby arrives. It also includes a brief question about self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe. Your answers stay completely confidential between you and our team, and the goal is simply to understand how you’re coping so we can give you the best support possible.

The EPDS is just ten straightforward questions about how you’ve felt in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever’s true for you. When you’re ready, we can start with the first one.

Here we go: In the past week, have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

[soft exhale, eyes down for a second]

Honestly… it’s been hard. Most of the time when my partner or my mom tries to joke, I just can’t feel it. I’ll give a little smile so they don’t worry, but inside it feels flat, like nothing’s funny anymore. Maybe once or twice I’ve managed a real laugh—like when the baby made that silly milk bubble—but even that faded fast and I felt guilty for enjoying anything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

No… not really. I mean, I *try*—I’ll force a little laugh if someone cracks a joke, but it feels fake. Most of the time nothing feels funny; it’s like the joy is stuck behind a wall.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]

Not much. Before the baby I’d get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even a new show. Now when I think about plans I mostly feel… blank, or worried it’ll be too hard. Once in a while I’ll look forward to a quiet moment when she’s asleep, but the bigger stuff feels pointless.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[sighs, eyes welling]

Yeah... a lot. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—my milk isn’t good enough, I’m holding her wrong, I missed her cues. Last night she wouldn’t settle and I kept replaying the whole day, convinced it was my fault for drinking that one cup of coffee. I know, rationally, babies cry, but the guilt just sits on my chest.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap]

Yes… pretty much every day. My heart races over things that don’t even have a real reason—like if the stroller shade is covering her face just right, or whether the formula is exactly the right temperature. I’ll check her breathing over and over, and still I can’t shake the fear that something bad’s about to happen. Even when she’s napping, I can’t relax; my mind keeps spinning through awful “what-ifs.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[fidgets with edge of sleeve]

Yeah… a few times this week. It hits out of nowhere—my chest gets tight, heart pounds, and suddenly I’m sure something terrible is about to happen even though nothing’s wrong. Like yesterday, I was just folding her onesies and this wave of panic rushed in. I had to sit down and keep telling myself “she’s fine, you’re fine,” but it took a while before the shaking stopped.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a shaky breath]

Most days, yeah. Feeding, changing, trying to sleep, the never-ending laundry of tiny socks… it all feels like a wave that keeps knocking me down. Sometimes I look at the pile of dishes and just want to sit on the floor and cry because I don’t know where to start. I manage—she’s always fed and clean—but I feel like I’m drowning in the small stuff and barely keeping my head up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[runs hand through hair, voice tired]

That’s been me almost every night this week. I lie down and my head just spins with all the “what-ifs” and regrets from the day. I’ll stare at the ceiling for an hour, then jerk awake when the baby makes the tiniest noise. Even when she sleeps a four-hour stretch, I can’t settle—I keep checking the monitor, convinced something’s wrong. By the time I drift off, it feels like minutes before she’s up again.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes drop to the floor, voice small]

Yeah… most of the day, most days. It’s this heavy, gray feeling that just sits there. I’ll be feeding her and tears start sliding down without me even realizing. Everything feels muted, like I’m watching life through dirty glass. There are little breaks—if she smiles in her sleep or grabs my finger—but the sadness always creeps back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods slowly, eyes glistening]

A couple of times this week. It’s not all-day sobbing, but it builds up—like yesterday when she wouldn’t nap and I felt so useless, I just sat in the rocker with her against my chest and cried quietly. And once at night, after everyone was asleep, the tears came and I couldn’t stop them for a while. It feels like the sadness needs to leak out somewhere.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, voice barely above a whisper]

Um… yeah, it’s flashed through my mind once or twice. Nothing planned—just this fleeting picture of “what if I weren’t here” when everything feels too heavy. I push it away fast because I’m scared of the thought, and I’d never want to leave her… but it did show up, and it frightened me.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS-style interview

**Symptoms endorsed**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt/worthlessness  
- Daily anxiety, situational panic attacks, intrusive “what-ifs”  
- Frequent crying, sadness described as “heavy, gray”  
- Sleep disturbance unrelated to infant needs  
- Feeling overwhelmed / unable to cope with routine tasks  
- Passive self-harm ideation (fleeting, no plan or intent)  

**Patterns / clinical significance**  
- Consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features, emerging in postpartum period  
- Severity sufficient to impair daily functioning and infant-care confidence  
- Safety concern level: passive suicidal cognition noted; requires immediate risk assessment and safety-planning  

**Risk factors highlighted**  
- Guilt about parenting competence; catastrophizing infant cues  
- Anxiety-driven checking / hypervigilance  
- Emotional lability and tearfulness  
- Sleep deprivation amplifying distress  
- Passive SI → red flag for suicide risk  

**Screening conclusion**  
Client scores high-risk for postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; reports passive self-harm thoughts. Recommend expedited referral for comprehensive psychiatric evaluation, safety planning, and appropriate psychosocial supports.
